```text
domain:
    # Spatial dimensions of A (from PolyBench NR, NQ, NP)
    r: dim in [0, NR)
    q: dim in [0, NQ)
    p: dim in [0, NP)
    # Reduction dimension over the innermost axis of A and the rows of C4
    s: dim in [0, NP)

data:
    # 3D array A, updated in place.
    # Layout matches PolyBench’s row-major A[NR][NQ][NP]:
    #   offset(i,j,k) = ((i * NQ) + j) * NP + k
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE =
        (r, q, p) -> (r * NQ + q) * NP + p

    # 2D transform matrix C4, read-only.
    # Layout matches PolyBench’s row-major C4[NP][NP]:
    #   offset(i,j) = i * NP + j
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # Logical accumulator vector for each (r, q).
    # In the optimized implementation this is *privatized per worker*
    # and typically realized as a stack-allocated or register-resident
    # tile of size O(NP) or O(TP), so total extra memory is
    # O(NP * num_threads) << O(NR * NQ * NP).
    acc[p]: scratch DATA_TYPE =
        (p) -> p

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match PolyBench macros)
    NR: int > 0
    NQ: int > 0
    NP: int > 0

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters
    TR: int > 0    # tile size along r  (e.g., 4–16)
    TQ: int > 0    # tile size along q  (e.g., 4–16)
    TS: int > 0    # tile size along s  (e.g., 16–64, fits L1/L2)
    TP: int > 0    # tile size along p  (e.g., 16–64, multiple of VP)
    VP: int > 0    # SIMD width along p (matches HW vector width)
    UR_S: int > 0  # unroll factor for s inside a tile

computation:
    # Mathematical semantics:
    # For each (r, q), A[r, q, :] is multiplied on the right by the
    # NP×NP matrix C4, using the original A[r, q, :] values as input.
    #
    # A_out[r, q, p] = Σ_{s=0..NP-1} A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # The explicit accumulator vector acc[p] in the Exo kernel is
    # just a concrete way of realizing this reduction while avoiding
    # read-after-write hazards on A.
    for r, q, p:
        A[r, q, p] = sum(s, A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

dependencies:
    # For each fixed (r, q, p), A[r, q, p] depends on:
    #   - all A[r, q, s] for s in [0, NP)
    #   - all C4[s, p]   for s in [0, NP)
    #
    # Different (r, q) pairs are completely independent and can be
    # computed in any order or in parallel.
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP):
        (A[r, q, *], C4[*, p]) -> A[r, q, p]

optimization:
    # -------------------------------
    # 1. Parallelism over (r, q)
    # -------------------------------
    # Tile the outer spatial dimensions and parallelize over tiles.
    # This distributes independent (r, q) blocks across cores while
    # reusing the small C4 matrix in cache.
    block(r, Rb, TR)      # Rb: tile index in r
    block(q, Qb, TQ)      # Qb: tile index in q
    parallelize(Rb)       # Run r-tiles in parallel across cores
    parallelize(Qb)       # May be implemented as a 2D parallel-for / collapse(2)

    # The accumulator acc[p] is *privatized per (r, q) tile* in the
    # concrete implementation (e.g., an OpenMP `private` array of
    # length NP or TP per worker), so there are no write conflicts.

    # -------------------------------
    # 2. Improve arithmetic intensity and locality
    # -------------------------------
    # The naive Exo version computes, conceptually:
    #   for r, q:
    #     for p:
    #       acc[p] = 0
    #       for s:
    #         acc[p] += A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # This reloads A[r, q, s] NP times (once per p) and walks C4
    # with a fixed column index (poor locality).
    #
    # Reordering inner loops to iterate over s first allows us to:
    #   - Load A[r, q, s] once per s and reuse it across all p.
    #   - Stream over rows of C4[s, :] with contiguous access.
    #
    # Reordered structure per (r, q):
    #   for p: acc[p] = 0
    #   for s:
    #     a_rs = A[r, q, s]
    #     for p:
    #       acc[p] += a_rs * C4[s, p]
    #
    # This is expressed as interchanging p and s in the inner nest.
    interchange(p, s)     # inside the (r, q) computation

    # -------------------------------
    # 3. Cache blocking of (s, p)
    # -------------------------------
    # Block the (s, p) plane so that:
    #   - A[r, q, s]-values and the corresponding C4[s, p] tiles
    #     fit nicely in L1/L2.
    #   - A tile of the accumulator acc[p] is kept in registers or
    #     in a very small stack buffer.
    block(s, Sb, TS)      # Sb: tile index over rows of C4 and A’s innermost dim
    block(p, Pb, TP)      # Pb: tile index over columns of C4 and A’s output dim

    # After blocking, the inner kernel structure for each (r, q, Sb, Pb)
    # is conceptually:
    #   for p in tile(Pb):
    #     acc[p] = 0   # only once per (r, q) or per tile, depending on strategy
    #   for s in tile(Sb):
    #     a_rs = A[r, q, s]
    #     for p in tile(Pb):
    #       acc[p] += a_rs * C4[s, p]
    #
    # and later:
    #   for p in tile(Pb):
    #     A[r, q, p] = acc[p]

    # Make the s-tile loop outer relative to the p-tile loop to
    # maximize reuse of A[r, q, s] and exploit row-major C4[s, p].
    hoist(Sb)

    # -------------------------------
    # 4. Micro-kernel tuning
    # -------------------------------
    # Within a (Sb, Pb) tile, tune the micro-kernel:
    unroll(s, UR_S)       # Unroll the inner s-loop within the tile
    vectorize(p, VP)      # SIMD over innermost p (contiguous in memory)

    # Implementation notes (informal, not part of the formal IR):
    # - acc[p] is implemented as:
    #     - a NP-element or TP-element array on the stack, marked
    #       `private` in parallel regions, or
    #     - a set of vector registers when TP == VP or TP is small
    #   so total extra memory is at most O(NP * num_threads),
    #   well below 50% of the original footprint.
    # - A[r, q, s] is loaded once per s-tile and broadcast across
    #   the vectorized p-loop, significantly reducing memory traffic
    #   compared to the original p-outer implementation.
```

domain:
    r: dim in [0, nr)
    q: dim in [0, nq)
    p: dim in [0, np)
    s: dim in [0, np)

data:
    # A is 3D: A[r][q][p], stored row-major as in PolyBench:
    #   A[r][q][p]  ↔  A_base[(r * nq + q) * np + p]
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE = (r, q, p) -> (r * nq + q) * np + p

    # C4 is 2D: C4[s][p], stored row-major:
    #   C4[s][p]  ↔  C4_base[s * np + p]
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE = (s, p) -> s * np + p

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (chosen to fit the cache hierarchy and SIMD width).
    R_TILE: int      # tile size for r (outermost dimension)
    Q_TILE: int      # tile size for q
    VEC_WIDTH: int   # SIMD width in elements for vectorization along p
    UNROLL_S: int    # unroll factor for the s (reduction) loop

computation:
    # For each (r, q), A[r, q, :] is a length-np row vector.
    # The kernel computes:
    #   A_new[r, q, p] = sum_{s=0}^{np-1} A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # This matches the original Exo code:
    #   sum[p] = 0
    #   for s: sum[p] += A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #   A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # Here we express it directly as a reduction; the temporary `sum[p]`
    # is an implementation detail and not part of the logical state.
    for r, q, p:
        A[r, q, p] = sum(s, A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

optimization:
    # --- 1. Exploit independence across (r, q) for multi-core parallelism. ---

    # Tile r and q so that each thread works on a rectangular block of rows
    # A[r, q, :] that fits well in cache.
    block(r, R, R_TILE)
    block(q, Q, Q_TILE)

    # Hoist the tile loops so they enclose the full inner computation.
    hoist(R)
    hoist(Q)

    # Parallelize across R tiles: different R-tiles (groups of r indices) are
    # fully independent because A[r, q, *] for different r never overlap and
    # C4 is read-only.
    parallelize(R)
    # (Optionally, if nr * nq is very large and tiles are large enough,
    #  Q could also be parallelized; left sequential here to avoid
    #  oversubscription.)
    # parallelize(Q)

    # --- 2. Choose a cache- and SIMD-friendly loop order for the core math. ---

    # Conceptually, inside each (r, q) block we use the schedule:
    #
    #   # initialize a private accumulation vector for this (r, q)
    #   for p in [0, np):
    #       acc[p] = 0
    #
    #   # reduction over s (matrix–vector product)
    #   for s in [0, np):
    #       a_rs = A[r, q, s]
    #       for p in [0, np):
    #           acc[p] += a_rs * C4[s, p]
    #
    #   # write back
    #   for p in [0, np):
    #       A[r, q, p] = acc[p]
    #
    # This keeps:
    #   - A[r, q, s] streamed once over s (good spatial locality on A),
    #   - C4[s, p] accessed row-wise (p is contiguous, good for cache & SIMD),
    #   - acc[p] reused across all s (held in registers/L1).
    #
    # The reduction operator `sum(s, ...)` already allows this reordering,
    # so we just document the intended innermost order via vectorization
    # and unrolling directives on p and s.

    # Vectorize along p: C4[s, p] is contiguous in p, so we can load a row of
    # C4 and a slice of acc[p] as SIMD vectors and perform vector FMA:
    #   acc_vec += a_rs * C4_row_vec
    vectorize(p, VEC_WIDTH)

    # Unroll the reduction over s to reduce loop overhead and expose ILP in the
    # FMA pipeline. We keep s sequential (no parallel reduce) to preserve a
    # well-defined accumulation order per p, matching the scalar semantics.
    unroll(s, UNROLL_S)

```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)
    q: dim in [0, NQ)
    p: dim in [0, NP)
    s: dim in [0, NP)

data:
    # 3D array A: input and output.
    # Row-major layout: p (last index) is contiguous, then q, then r.
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE =
        (r, q, p) -> r * (NQ * NP) + q * NP + p

    # 2D array C4: constant coefficient matrix.
    # Row-major layout: p (last index) is contiguous.
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # Scratch vector "sum" is *not* part of the external interface.
    # It is introduced as a per-(r, q) temporary in the optimization section
    # and can be implemented as a thread-private stack buffer of length NP.

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (passed as nr, nq, np in the C/Exo code).
    NR: size
    NQ: size
    NP: size

computation:
    # Semantics: for each (r, q), overwrite the length-NP row A[r, q, :]
    # with the product of the original row and the NP×NP matrix C4:
    #
    #   A_new[r, q, p] = sum_{s=0..NP-1} A_old[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # where A_old denotes the value of A at kernel entry.
    # This matches the Exo kernel’s behavior, which uses a temporary
    # vector `sum[p]` and then copies it back into A[r, q, p].
    for r, q, p:
        A[r, q, p] = sum(s, A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

optimization:
    # High-level view:
    #   - For each (r, q) slice, we are doing a dense row-vector × matrix
    #     product:  (1 × NP) * (NP × NP) → (1 × NP).
    #   - The natural implementation is to introduce a temporary vector
    #     sum[p] that holds the new row before we overwrite A in place.
    #
    # Per-(r, q) optimized skeleton (semantic rewrite of the reduction order):
    #   sum[p] = 0          # for all p in [0, NP)
    #   for s in [0, NP):
    #       a = A[r, q, s]  # loaded once per s and reused across all p
    #       for p in [0, NP):
    #           sum[p] += a * C4[s, p]
    #   for p in [0, NP):
    #       A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # This reorders the original (p, s) nest into (s, p) with an explicit
    # temporary:
    #   - A[r, q, s] is read once per (r, q, s), instead of NP times.
    #   - C4[s, p] is traversed row-wise (p contiguous) in the inner loop,
    #     matching its row-major layout.
    #   - Using sum[p] ensures we never read a partially updated A[r, q, s],
    #     preserving the in-place semantics.

    # Introduce a per-(r, q) scratch vector sum[p] of length NP.
    # This is conceptually:
    #   sum[p]: scratch DATA_TYPE, p in [0, NP)
    # but implemented as a thread-private buffer reused across (r, q).
    # Memory usage is O(NP), which is small relative to A (O(NR·NQ·NP))
    # and well within the 50% overhead guideline for realistic sizes.
    # (No extra NR·NQ·NP-sized buffer is introduced.)

    # 1. Tile the independent outer work over r and q for cache locality
    #    and coarse-grain parallelism.
    block(r, R, TR)     # TR: tunable tile size in r  (e.g., 8–64)
    block(q, Q, TQ)     # TQ: tunable tile size in q  (e.g., 4–32)
    hoist(R)            # Make R the outermost loop
    hoist(Q)            # Make Q the next-outermost loop

    # 2. Inside each (R, Q) tile, implement the skeleton above:
    #    for r in tile R:
    #      for q in tile Q:
    #        sum[p] = 0          # vector initialization
    #        for s:
    #          a = A[r, q, s]
    #          for p:
    #            sum[p] += a * C4[s, p]
    #        for p:
    #          A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # We now optimize the inner (s, p) loops.

    # 3. Block the p-dimension to improve locality for sum[p] and C4[s, p],
    #    and to enable efficient SIMD on contiguous chunks.
    block(p, P, TP)     # TP: tunable tile size for p (e.g., 32–256)

    # After blocking, a typical inner structure (per r, q) is:
    #   for P in tiles of p:
    #     # initialize sum[p] for this P-tile
    #     for p in P:
    #       sum[p] = 0
    #     for s in [0, NP):
    #       a = A[r, q, s]
    #       for p in P:
    #         sum[p] += a * C4[s, p]
    #     for p in P:
    #       A[r, q, p] = sum[p]

    # 4. Parallelize across the outer tiles (R, Q).
    #    Each (R, Q) tile updates a disjoint block of A and uses its own
    #    thread-private sum[p], while C4 is read-only, so there are no
    #    cross-thread dependencies.
    parallelize(R)      # Distribute r-tiles across threads
    parallelize(Q)      # Optionally further decompose across q-tiles

    # 5. Vectorize and unroll the innermost p-loop within each P-tile.
    #    This exploits that:
    #      - sum[p] and C4[s, p] are contiguous in p,
    #      - iterations over p are independent for fixed (r, q, s).
    vectorize(p, VP)    # VP: SIMD width (e.g., 8 or 16), chosen for the target
    unroll(p, UF)       # UF: small unroll factor (e.g., 2–4) for extra ILP

    # 6. Optionally unroll the reduction over s for additional ILP
    #    when NP is small to moderate.
    unroll(s, US)       # US: tunable s-unroll factor (careful with registers)

    # Notes:
    # - No change in data layout is required: both A[r, q, s] (in s) and
    #   C4[s, p] (in p) are accessed along their row-major contiguous
    #   dimensions in the hot loops.
    # - The critical arithmetic count remains NR * NQ * NP^2 multiplies
    #   and adds; we only reduce redundant loads and improve locality.
    # - The outer (R, Q) tiles and inner (P, s, p) structure expose ample
    #   parallel and vector parallelism while respecting the original
    #   in-place semantics of A.
```

```text
domain:
    # Problem sizes (PolyBench DOITGEN)
    r: dim in [0, NR)        # row index in the first spatial dimension
    q: dim in [0, NQ)        # row index in the second spatial dimension
    p: dim in [0, NP)        # output coordinate within each (r,q) line
    s: dim in [0, NP)        # reduction coordinate over the input line

data:
    # 3D array A, updated in-place.
    # C layout: A[r][q][p] with p as the fastest-varying index (row-major).
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, p) -> (r * NQ + q) * NP + p

    # 2D transform matrix C4, read-only.
    # C layout: C4[s][p] with p as the fastest-varying index (row-major).
    # After scheduling, we will traverse C4 by rows (s fixed, p innermost),
    # which matches this layout and gives unit-stride loads.
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE
        = (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # Logical temporary used per (r,q) to hold the transformed line.
    # In the original Exo kernel this is the array `sum[np]` passed in;
    # in an optimized implementation this is best realized as a stack- or
    # thread-local buffer reused across (r,q) iterations.
    tmp_row[p]: local DATA_TYPE
        = p -> p   # contiguous 1D layout

parameters:
    # NR, NQ, NP are the problem sizes (compile-time or run-time).
    # The remaining parameters are tunable constants for performance.

    R_TILE: int    # tile size in r, e.g., 4 or 8
    Q_TILE: int    # tile size in q, e.g., 4 or 8
    P_TILE: int    # tile size in p, e.g., 32 or 64
    VEC_WIDTH: int # SIMD width (elements per vector), e.g., 4 or 8
    S_UNROLL: int  # unroll factor for the reduction over s, e.g., 4

computation:
    # Semantics: for each (r,q,p) we compute
    #   A_new[r,q,p] = sum_s A_old[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    # but we must not overwrite A[r,q,*] until all RHS values for this (r,q)
    # have been computed. We therefore compute into tmp_row first,
    # then copy back into A. This matches the original Exo code, which
    # accumulates into `sum[p]` and only later writes A[r,q,p] = sum[p].

    for r, q:
        # 1) Compute the transformed line tmp_row[p] = Σ_s A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p].
        # Expressed mathematically with an explicit reduction:
        for p:
            tmp_row[p] = sum(s, A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

        # 2) Overwrite A in-place only after the whole line is available.
        for p:
            A[r, q, p] = tmp_row[p]

optimization:
    # High-level view:
    #   - For each fixed (r,q), A[r,q,*] is a 1×NP row-vector.
    #   - C4 is an NP×NP matrix.
    #   - The computation is a row–matrix product:
    #         tmp_row[·] = A[r,q,·] * C4
    #     and then A[r,q,·] := tmp_row[·].
    #
    # The original Exo kernel computes one output coordinate p at a time:
    #   for p:          # outer
    #     sum[p] = 0
    #     for s:
    #       sum[p] += A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    #   for p:
    #     A[r,q,p] = sum[p]
    #
    # This keeps good locality for A (s is the fastest-varying index of A)
    # but accesses C4 with a large stride (varying s across rows while p is
    # fixed in the inner loop). We instead compute all p simultaneously
    # for each s, so that we stream contiguous rows of C4.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Re-express the per-(r,q) computation as a matrix–vector product
    #    with s outermost and p innermost.
    #
    #    For each (r,q), use the following concrete loop structure:
    #
    #        # zero accumulation vector once per (r,q)
    #        for p in [0, NP):
    #            tmp_row[p] = 0
    #
    #        # reduction over s; p innermost for unit-stride C4 access
    #        for s in [0, NP):
    #            a_rqs = A[r, q, s]          # scalar reused across p
    #            for p in [0, NP):
    #                tmp_row[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #
    #        # write back the completed line
    #        for p in [0, NP):
    #            A[r, q, p] = tmp_row[p]
    #
    #    This is algebraically equivalent to tmp_row[p] = sum_s A[r,q,s]*C4[s,p],
    #    but:
    #      - A[r,q,s] is read once per s (not once per (p,s)),
    #      - C4[s,p] is read with p as the innermost index (row-major, unit stride),
    #      - tmp_row[p] stays in L1/L2 (and often in registers via vectorization).

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Tile the outer spatial dimensions (r, q) to form coarse-grain
    #    work units that can be distributed across cores.

    block(r, Rb, R_TILE)
    # r = Rb * R_TILE + r_in_tile, where r_in_tile is the new inner r index.

    block(q, Qb, Q_TILE)
    # q = Qb * Q_TILE + q_in_tile.

    hoist(Rb)
    hoist(Qb)
    # After hoisting, the outer loop order is:
    #   for Rb in [0, ceil(NR / R_TILE)):
    #     for Qb in [0, ceil(NQ / Q_TILE)):
    #       for r_in_tile:
    #         for q_in_tile:
    #           ... per-(r,q) computation ...

    # Parallelize over r-tiles (and thus over blocks of (r,q)).
    parallelize(Rb)
    # Each worker thread handles a strip of R_TILE rows (and all Q_TILE columns
    # within each Qb). An implementation may additionally parallelize Qb or
    # collapse (Rb, Qb) if finer-grain parallelism is needed, but the key is
    # that different (r,q) pairs are independent so no synchronization is
    # required beyond the outer parallel region.

    # tmp_row[p] is thread-local (or allocated on the stack inside the
    # parallel region), so there are no races on the accumulation buffer and
    # the additional memory is O(NP) per thread, which is negligible compared
    # to O(NR*NQ*NP) for A and O(NP*NP) for C4.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Optimize the inner matrix–vector product by tiling and vectorizing
    #    along the p dimension while keeping s as the reduction dimension.

    # Tile p to improve cache locality for tmp_row and C4, and to expose a
    # natural unit for SIMD vectorization.
    block(p, Pb, P_TILE)
    # p = Pb * P_TILE + p_in_tile.

    # Hoist Pb outside the reduction over s so that we process each tile
    # in p independently:
    #
    #   for Pb:
    #     # zero tmp_row on this tile
    #     for p_in_tile:
    #         tmp_row[p] = 0
    #
    #     for s:
    #         a_rqs = A[r,q,s]
    #         for p_in_tile:
    #             tmp_row[p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    #
    #     for p_in_tile:
    #         A[r,q,p] = tmp_row[p]
    #
    # Because different p values are independent, this tiling over p preserves
    # semantics while limiting the working set of tmp_row and C4 per inner loop.

    hoist(Pb)

    # Vectorize the innermost p loop over the tile. Since C4 is row-major and
    # p is the fastest-varying index, this produces aligned, unit-stride loads
    # from C4 and tmp_row, and lets the compiler generate fused multiply–add
    # (FMA) instructions for the reduction.
    vectorize(p, VEC_WIDTH)

    # Unroll the reduction over s by a small factor to increase ILP and let the
    # compiler schedule multiple independent FMAs per iteration. The unroll
    # factor S_UNROLL is a tuning parameter (e.g., 2, 4, or 8) chosen such that
    # the inner working set still fits in registers.
    unroll(s, S_UNROLL)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Data layout considerations.
    #
    # - A is already laid out with p as the fastest-varying index, and in the
    #   optimized schedule we access A[r,q,s] with s as the fastest-varying
    #   loop variable. This is unit-stride and cache-friendly.
    #
    # - C4 is stored row-major as C4[s,p], and the optimized schedule traverses
    #   C4 with s outer, p inner (and with p tiled). This is also unit-stride
    #   along p, so no change of layout (e.g., transposition) is required.
    #
    # As a result, no additional large temporary buffers are introduced; only
    # tmp_row[p] of size NP (per thread) is used, matching or modestly
    # exceeding the original sum[np] buffer but still well within the
    # 50% memory overhead constraint relative to A and C4.
```

```text
domain:
    # Dimensions correspond to the PolyBench problem sizes.
    r: dim in [0, NR)   # row index   of A
    q: dim in [0, NQ)   # column index of A (2nd dim)
    p: dim in [0, NP)   # output index within the fastest-varying dim of A
    s: dim in [0, NP)   # reduction index over the fastest-varying dim of A

data:
    # 3D array A[r,q,p], row-major: p is fastest-varying.
    # Underlying linear index: ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

    # 2D transform matrix C4[s,p], row-major: p is fastest-varying.
    # Underlying linear index: s * NP + p
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE = (s, p) -> s * NP + p

    # 1D temporary accumulation buffer, same as the C `sum` array.
    # It is reinitialized for each (r,q) pair and only its final value
    # for the last (r,q) is externally observable (as in the original code).
    sum[p]: inout DATA_TYPE = p  # used as scratch workspace

computation:
    # For each (r, q), we conceptually compute:
    #   newA[r, q, p] = sum_s A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    # and then overwrite A[r, q, p] with newA[r, q, p].
    #
    # Compared to the original kernel, we restructure the inner loops to:
    #   - load A[r,q,s] once per s and reuse across all p
    #   - traverse C4[s,*] as a contiguous row
    # while preserving:
    #   sum[p] = Σ_s A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]    for every (r,q,p).

    for r, q:
        # 1) Initialize the accumulation buffer for this (r,q) slice.
        for p:
            sum[p] = 0.0

        # 2) Accumulate contributions from each source index s.
        #    This is a matrix–vector product: A[r,q,:] (length NP)
        #    times the NP×NP matrix C4.
        for s:
            a_rqs = A[r, q, s]          # scalar reused across all p
            for p:
                sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]

        # 3) Commit the accumulated result back into A.
        for p:
            A[r, q, p] = sum[p]

optimization:
    # The computation above already reflects the key semantic-preserving
    # loop transformation:
    #   - In the original kernel, the order under (r,q) was:
    #         for p:
    #             sum[p] = 0
    #             for s:
    #                 sum[p] += A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    #         for p:
    #             A[r,q,p] = sum[p]
    #   - Here we:
    #       * separate zeroing of sum[p] from the accumulation
    #       * interchange the p and s loops in the accumulation
    #     yielding:
    #         for p: sum[p] = 0
    #         for s:
    #             a_rqs = A[r,q,s]
    #             for p: sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s,p]
    #         for p: A[r,q,p] = sum[p]
    #   This preserves:
    #       sum[p] = Σ_s A[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    #     but improves locality:
    #       - A[r,q,s] is loaded once per s instead of NP times
    #       - C4[s,*] is traversed as a contiguous row.

    # --- Cache- and TLB-friendly outer blocking ---

    # Block the outer (r, q) loops to improve temporal locality on A and C4
    # and to control the working set per tile. TR and TQ are tunable tile sizes,
    # chosen such that the data for a tile fits comfortably into L2/L3.
    block(r, R, TR)             # r = R * TR + r_in
    block(q, Q, TQ)             # q = Q * TQ + q_in
    hoist(R)                    # move tile loop R to the outermost position
    hoist(Q)                    # nest tile loop Q just inside R
    # The resulting execution order still visits all (r,q) in a deterministic
    # lexicographic order ending at (NR-1, NQ-1), so the final contents of
    # sum[] and A match the original kernel.

    # --- SIMD vectorization along the contiguous p dimension ---

    # Within each fixed (r, q, s), the innermost loop over p walks contiguous
    # elements of both sum[p] and C4[s,p]. This is ideal for SIMD.
    # VP is a hardware-tuned vector width (e.g., 4 or 8 on x86 with AVX/AVX2).
    vectorize(p, VP)

    # --- Optional unrolling for additional ILP ---

    # For small to moderate NP, unrolling further exposes instruction-level
    # parallelism and reduces loop-control overhead. UP_p and UP_s are
    # small integer factors (e.g., 2–4) tuned empirically.
    unroll(p, UP_p)
    unroll(s, UP_s)
```
